summary: Blonanserin is a second-generation (atypical) antipsychotic of the dopamine-serotonin antagonist (DSA) class, used to treat schizophrenia. It is approved in Japan (PMDA), South Korea, India and some other countries but is NOT FDA-approved (this record is based on PMDA/Asian labeling and is pending clinical review). The usual oral dose starts at 4 mg twice daily after meals, with a usual range of 8-16 mg/day and a maximum of 24 mg/day; a transdermal patch is also marketed in Japan. Unusually for an atypical, it has higher affinity for dopamine D2/D3 than for serotonin 5-HT2A receptors. It must be taken after food because absorption is markedly increased by meals, and it is a CYP3A4 substrate so strong CYP3A4 inhibitors (e.g. azole antifungals) are contraindicated. As an antipsychotic it carries the class warning of increased mortality in elderly patients with dementia-related psychosis; extrapyramidal symptoms/akathisia are the most prominent adverse effects, with comparatively modest weight gain, sedation, and prolactin elevation.

moa: Blonanserin is a serotonin-dopamine antagonist with potent antagonist activity at dopamine D2 and D3 receptors and at serotonin 5-HT2A receptors. In contrast to most atypical antipsychotics, its affinity for D2 receptors is higher than for 5-HT2A receptors (hence sometimes termed a 'dopamine-serotonin antagonist'). Antagonism of mesolimbic D2 receptors reduces positive psychotic symptoms, while 5-HT2A blockade and a degree of D3 antagonism are thought to contribute to effects on negative and cognitive symptoms and to a relatively favourable extrapyramidal profile at lower doses. It has low affinity for histaminergic, adrenergic, and muscarinic receptors, accounting for relatively modest weight gain, sedation, and anticholinergic effects.

absolute: Known hypersensitivity to blonanserin or excipients
Concomitant use with strong CYP3A4 inhibitors - azole antifungals (itraconazole), HIV protease inhibitors (ritonavir, etc.) (markedly raise blonanserin levels)
Adrenaline (epinephrine) administration except for anaphylaxis (reversal of pressor effect)
relative: Elderly with dementia-related psychosis (increased mortality and cerebrovascular events - antipsychotic class effect)
Cardiovascular disease, QT prolongation, or risk of arrhythmia
History of seizures / conditions lowering seizure threshold
Hypotension or risk of orthostatic hypotension

preg: Safety in pregnancy is not established. As with other antipsychotics, neonates exposed during the third trimester are at risk of extrapyramidal and/or withdrawal symptoms (agitation, hypertonia/hypotonia, tremor, somnolence, respiratory distress, feeding difficulty). Use during pregnancy only if the expected benefit justifies the potential risk, and monitor exposed neonates.
lact: Blonanserin is excreted in the milk of lactating animals; human data are limited. Breastfeeding is not recommended during treatment because of the potential for adverse effects in the infant.
renal: There is limited information on use in renal impairment. Use with caution and monitor; consider lower doses and careful titration in significant impairment.
hepatic: Blonanserin is metabolised by the liver (CYP3A4). In hepatic impairment, plasma levels may rise - use with caution, start low, titrate slowly, and monitor for adverse effects.

major: Strong CYP3A4 inhibitors - azole antifungals (itraconazole), HIV protease inhibitors (ritonavir) (contraindicated - markedly increased blonanserin exposure)
Adrenaline/epinephrine (blonanserin can reverse the pressor effect, causing severe hypotension - avoid except for anaphylaxis)
moderate: Moderate CYP3A4 inhibitors - erythromycin, diltiazem, grapefruit juice (raise levels)
CYP3A4 inducers - rifampin, carbamazepine, phenytoin (reduce blonanserin levels/efficacy)
Other CNS depressants and antihypertensives (additive sedation/hypotension)

Avoid grapefruit juice and tell your doctor about antifungal or HIV medicines (serious interactions)

pearls: NOT FDA-approved; approved in Japan (PMDA), South Korea, India and others - this record is based on PMDA/Asian labeling and is pending clinical review.
Atypical antipsychotic of the dopamine-serotonin antagonist (DSA) class - unusually, its D2/D3 affinity exceeds its 5-HT2A affinity.
MUST be taken after food - meals markedly increase its absorption; fasting administration gives sub-therapeutic, erratic levels.
CYP3A4 substrate - strong CYP3A4 inhibitors (azole antifungals, HIV protease inhibitors) are contraindicated; avoid grapefruit juice; adrenaline is contraindicated except for anaphylaxis.
Extrapyramidal symptoms/akathisia are the most prominent adverse effects, with comparatively modest weight gain, sedation, and metabolic burden.
Antipsychotic class warning: increased mortality in elderly patients with dementia-related psychosis; a transdermal patch formulation is also available in Japan.
missed: Take the missed dose after food as soon as you remember. If it is almost time for the next dose, skip the missed dose and continue your usual schedule - do not take a double dose. Keep dosing times consistent and always take with food.
overdose: Overdose exaggerates the pharmacology: drowsiness, sedation, extrapyramidal symptoms, hypotension, tachycardia, and potential QT prolongation/arrhythmia. There is no specific antidote. Manage supportively: secure the airway and support ventilation, give activated charcoal if early and airway protected, provide continuous cardiac/ECG monitoring, treat hypotension with IV fluids (avoid adrenaline, which can worsen hypotension - use noradrenaline if a pressor is needed), and give anticholinergics for severe extrapyramidal symptoms. Maintain monitoring until recovery.
